items.title: From FTP Deploys and Cron Scripts to a Real Pipeline
items.summary: Quick answer: Replace FTP deploys with Git-based atomic releases: build in CI, upload to a new timestamped release directory, symlink shared storage and .env, run migrations, then switch a "current" symlink. Move crontab entries one by one into Laravel's scheduler with locks and logging. Keep the old path working until each piece is proven. In Part 4 we moved auth and sessions without logging anyone out. The next thing that tends to break legacy modernization is not the code. It is how the code reaches the server. If production is "whatever someone last uploaded with FileZilla", you cannot reason about what is running, you cannot roll back, and the new Laravel modules from Parts 1–3 end up deployed the same fragile way. I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi, and at Loop Origin we inherit a lot of these apps. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked the commands against the Deployer, GitHub Actions and Laravel scheduler documentation. 📚 Series Navigation — Modernizing Legacy PHP Without a Rewrite Part 1: Strangler Fig for Legacy PHP: Run Old and New Side by Side Part 2: Untangling Dependency Cycles in a Modular Laravel Monolith Part 3: Upgrading Old PHP Versions Safely With Rector and CI Part 4: Replacing Legacy Auth & Sessions Without Logging Everyone Out Part 5 (This Post): From FTP Deploys and Cron Scripts to a Real Pipeline Part 6: Decommissioning the Old App: Shadow Traffic, Flags & Final Cutover Related earlier posts: Backups That Never Restored: Automated Restore Drills · Zero-Downtime Database Migrations in Laravel & Node.js SaaS Step 0: find out what production actually is Before changing anything, I take an inventory. It works for old procedural PHP and Laravel alike. { % raw % } ~~~text /var/www/app/ current - > releases/20261122-0715-a1b2c3d releases/ 20261121-1930-9f8e7d6/ 20261122-0715-a1b2c3d/ shared/ .env storage/ public/uploads/ ~~~ { % endraw % } Each release is a fresh checkout. Nginx points at { % raw % } `/var/www/app/current/public` { % endraw % } , and PHP-FPM is reloaded after the switch so OPcache drops stale paths. ## The CI pipeline I build artifacts in CI, not on the server. Here is a trimmed GitHub Actions workflow: { % raw % } ~~~yaml name: deploy on: push: branches: [ main ] jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: production # requires manual approval in repo settings steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2 with: { php-version: '8.3' } - run: composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader - run: vendor/bin/phpunit --testsuite=smoke - run: tar czf release.tgz --exclude=.git --exclude=tests . - name: Upload and activate env: SSH_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY } } run: ./deploy/activate.sh release.tgz "$GITHUB_SHA" ~~~ { % endraw % } The { % raw % } `activate.sh` { % endraw % } script is short and boring on purpose: { % raw % } ~~~bash #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail REL = "$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M)-$(echo " $2 " | cut -c1-7)" ssh deploy@app "mkdir -p /var/www/app/releases/$REL" scp "$1" deploy@app:/tmp/release.tgz ssh deploy@app bash -s << EOF set -e cd /var/www/app/releases/ $REL && tar xzf /tmp/release.tgz ln -sfn /var/www/app/shared/.env .env rm -rf storage && ln -sfn /var/www/app/shared/storage storage php artisan migrate --force php artisan config:cache && php artisan route:cache ln -sfn /var/www/app/releases/ $REL /var/www/app/current sudo systemctl reload php8.3-fpm ls -1dt /var/www/app/releases/* | tail -n +6 | xargs rm -rf # keep 5 EOF ~~~ { % endraw % } Two cautions. Later, each wrapped script can be rewritten as a proper command or queued job when someone actually needs to change it. ## Diagnostic checklist - [ ] Production web root diffed against Git ; hotfixes committed - [ ] Uploads, logs and caches moved to a shared directory outside releases - [ ] Secrets in a shared .env, not in committed config files - [ ] CI builds the artifact and runs at least a smoke test suite - [ ] Releases are timestamped directories with a { % raw % } `current` { % endraw % } symlink - [ ] PHP-FPM is reloaded after each switch - [ ] Rollback tested on staging this month - [ ] Crontab reduced to { % raw % } `schedule:run` { % endraw % } , every job has locking and logs - [ ] FTP access disabled once the pipeline is proven ## FAQ ### Can I do this on shared hosting without SSH? Partly. Many hosts now offer SSH or Git deploy. If yours has neither, that is a strong reason to move to a small VPS ; atomic releases depend on symlinks and shell access. ### What about apps that write files into the code directory? Find every write path first, from the inventory step, and point them at { % raw % } `shared/` { % endraw % } . Until that is done, atomic releases will lose user data on each deploy. ### Do I need Docker for this? No. Containers are a fine next step, but release directories plus CI give you most of the safety with far less change to an old app. ### How do I handle the first deploy safely? Deploy the pipeline 's first release to a new path, point a staging hostname at it, compare behaviour, then switch Nginx for production. Keep the old document root intact for a week. ### What if a cron job must never run twice? Use `withoutOverlapping` with a reasonable expiry, `onOneServer` when you have more than one app server, and make the script itself idempotent where you can. ### When can I turn off FTP? After two or three clean pipeline deploys and one tested rollback. Quick answer: Replace FTP deploys with Git-based atomic releases: build in CI, upload to a new timestamped release directory, symlink shared storage and .env, run migrations, then switch a "current" symlink. Move crontab entries one by one into Laravel's scheduler with locks and logging. Keep the old path working until each piece is proven.

In Part 4 we moved auth and sessions without logging anyone out. The next thing that tends to break legacy modernization is not the code. It is how the code reaches the server. If production is "whatever someone last uploaded with FileZilla", you cannot reason about what is running, you cannot roll back, and the new Laravel modules from Parts 1–3 end up deployed the same fragile way.

I am a Principal Software Engineer in Karachi, and at Loop Origin we inherit a lot of these apps. I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked the commands against the Deployer, GitHub Actions and Laravel scheduler documentation.

📚 Series Navigation — Modernizing Legacy PHP Without a Rewrite

  • Part 1: Strangler Fig for Legacy PHP: Run Old and New Side by Side
  • Part 2: Untangling Dependency Cycles in a Modular Laravel Monolith
  • Part 3: Upgrading Old PHP Versions Safely With Rector and CI
  • Part 4: Replacing Legacy Auth & Sessions Without Logging Everyone Out
  • Part 5 (This Post): From FTP Deploys and Cron Scripts to a Real Pipeline
  • Part 6: Decommissioning the Old App: Shadow Traffic, Flags & Final Cutover

Related earlier posts: Backups That Never Restored: Automated Restore Drills · Zero-Downtime Database Migrations in Laravel & Node.js SaaS

Step 0: find out what production actually is

Before changing anything, I take an inventory. Production often differs from any repository you were given.

# On the server, read-only
cd /var/www/legacy-app
find . -type f -newer composer.json -not -path "./storage/*" | head -50   # files edited after last known deploy
crontab -l -u www-data > ~/cron-inventory.txt
sudo ls /etc/cron.d/ >> ~/cron-inventory.txt
php -v; php -m > ~/php-modules.txt
~~~{% endraw %}

Then I download a full copy of the web root and diff it against the repository. Every difference is either a hotfix that never got committed (commit it) or junk like {% raw %}`index_old2.php`{% endraw %} (note it and remove it later). Uploaded user files and generated caches get listed separately; they must never live inside the code directory again.

## FTP deploys vs a real pipeline

| Concern | FTP / manual upload | Atomic release pipeline |
|---|---|---|
| What is running? | Unknown mix of files | One Git commit SHA per release |
| Half-uploaded state | Yes, for minutes | No, symlink switch is instant |
| Rollback | Re-upload old files from memory | Point symlink to previous release |
| Dependencies | Vendor folder uploaded by hand | {% raw %}`composer install --no-dev`{% endraw %} in CI |
| Secrets | Edited live in config.php | Shared .env outside releases |
| Audit trail | None | CI run, commit, who approved |

## The release directory layout

This is the layout I use on plain VPS servers. It works for old procedural PHP and Laravel alike.{% raw %}

~~~text
/var/www/app/
  current -> releases/20261122-0715-a1b2c3d
  releases/
    20261121-1930-9f8e7d6/
    20261122-0715-a1b2c3d/
  shared/
    .env
    storage/
    public/uploads/
~~~{% endraw %}

Each release is a fresh checkout. Shared folders and the env file are symlinked into it. Nginx points at {% raw %}`/var/www/app/current/public`{% endraw %}, and PHP-FPM is reloaded after the switch so OPcache drops stale paths.

## The CI pipeline

I build artifacts in CI, not on the server. Here is a trimmed GitHub Actions workflow:{% raw %}

~~~yaml
name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production        # requires manual approval in repo settings
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.3' }
      - run: composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader
      - run: vendor/bin/phpunit --testsuite=smoke
      - run: tar czf release.tgz --exclude=.git --exclude=tests .
      - name: Upload and activate
        env:
          SSH_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }}
        run: ./deploy/activate.sh release.tgz "$GITHUB_SHA"
~~~{% endraw %}

The {% raw %}`activate.sh`{% endraw %} script is short and boring on purpose:{% raw %}

~~~bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
REL="$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M)-$(echo "$2" | cut -c1-7)"
ssh deploy@app "mkdir -p /var/www/app/releases/$REL"
scp "$1" deploy@app:/tmp/release.tgz
ssh deploy@app bash -s <<EOF
set -e
cd /var/www/app/releases/$REL && tar xzf /tmp/release.tgz
ln -sfn /var/www/app/shared/.env .env
rm -rf storage && ln -sfn /var/www/app/shared/storage storage
php artisan migrate --force
php artisan config:cache && php artisan route:cache
ln -sfn /var/www/app/releases/$REL /var/www/app/current
sudo systemctl reload php8.3-fpm
ls -1dt /var/www/app/releases/* | tail -n +6 | xargs rm -rf   # keep 5
EOF
~~~{% endraw %}

Two cautions. Migrations run before the switch, so they must be backward compatible with the release still serving traffic; that is the expand-and-contract pattern from my zero-downtime migrations post. And keep the deploy user's sudo rights limited to reloading PHP-FPM, nothing else. If you would rather use a tool, Deployer does the same release/symlink dance with less shell.

## Rollback is one command{% raw %}

~~~bash
ssh deploy@app 'cd /var/www/app && PREV=$(ls -1dt releases/* | sed -n 2p) && ln -sfn "$PWD/$PREV" current && sudo systemctl reload php8.3-fpm'
~~~

Rollback does not undo database migrations. That is another reason to keep migrations additive until the old code is gone.

## Taming the crontab

Old apps hide business logic in cron: invoice emails at 2 a.m., a CSV import every 10 minutes, a cleanup script that nobody dares touch. My rule is to move them one at a time into Laravel's scheduler, wrapping the old script first rather than rewriting it.{% raw %}

~~~php
// routes/console.php (Laravel 11+)
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schedule;

Schedule::exec('php /var/www/app/current/legacy/cron/send_invoices.php')
    ->dailyAt('02:00')
    ->timezone('Asia/Karachi')
    ->withoutOverlapping(30)
    ->onOneServer()
    ->appendOutputTo(storage_path('logs/cron-send-invoices.log'))
    ->onFailure(fn () => report(new RuntimeException('send_invoices failed')));
~~~{% endraw %}

Then the crontab shrinks to a single line, {% raw %}`* * * * * php /var/www/app/current/artisan schedule:run`{% endraw %}. For each migrated job I disable the old crontab line in the same change, never before and never after, so it cannot run twice or not at all. {% raw %}`withoutOverlapping`{% endraw %} fixes the classic bug where a slow import starts again before the last one finished. Later, each wrapped script can be rewritten as a proper command or queued job when someone actually needs to change it.

## Diagnostic checklist

- [ ] Production web root diffed against Git; hotfixes committed
- [ ] Uploads, logs and caches moved to a shared directory outside releases
- [ ] Secrets in a shared .env, not in committed config files
- [ ] CI builds the artifact and runs at least a smoke test suite
- [ ] Releases are timestamped directories with a {% raw %}`current`{% endraw %} symlink
- [ ] PHP-FPM is reloaded after each switch
- [ ] Rollback tested on staging this month
- [ ] Crontab reduced to {% raw %}`schedule:run`{% endraw %}, every job has locking and logs
- [ ] FTP access disabled once the pipeline is proven

## FAQ

### Can I do this on shared hosting without SSH?
Partly. Many hosts now offer SSH or Git deploy. If yours has neither, that is a strong reason to move to a small VPS; atomic releases depend on symlinks and shell access.

### What about apps that write files into the code directory?
Find every write path first, from the inventory step, and point them at {% raw %}`shared/`{% endraw %}. Until that is done, atomic releases will lose user data on each deploy.

### Do I need Docker for this?
No. Containers are a fine next step, but release directories plus CI give you most of the safety with far less change to an old app.

### How do I handle the first deploy safely?
Deploy the pipeline's first release to a new path, point a staging hostname at it, compare behaviour, then switch Nginx for production. Keep the old document root intact for a week.

### What if a cron job must never run twice?
Use `withoutOverlapping` with a reasonable expiry, `onOneServer` when you have more than one app server, and make the script itself idempotent where you can.

### When can I turn off FTP?
After two or three clean pipeline deploys and one tested rollback. Remove the FTP accounts rather than just changing passwords.

## What's next

Part 6, the finale, covers decommissioning the old app: shadow traffic, feature flags and the final cutover. items.title: Break-Glass Accounts & SSO Audit Logs
items.summary: Quick answer: A break-glass account is a tightly limited local login that still works when a tenant's SSO fails. Keep one or two per tenant, protect them with a hardware-key MFA factor, alert on every use, and expire their sessions fast. Log every SSO event with tenant, subject, result and reason, in UTC, hash-chained so tampering shows. Enforced SSO is the goal of most enterprise deals. Then one morning the customer's certificate rotates, or their Entra ID tenant has an outage, or an admin deletes the app assignment by mistake, and 400 people cannot reach your product. If enforced SSO means there is no other way in, you now have a support incident you cannot fix from your side without bypassing your own security. Break-glass access and good audit logs are the two pieces that make enforced SSO safe to sell. This last part of the series covers both. I wrote it with help from AI tools and checked it against NIST SP 800-63B guidance on authenticators and the Okta and Microsoft Entra ID documentation on emergency access accounts. Everything here is defensive design for your own application. 📚 Series Navigation — Enterprise SSO & Identity for B2B SaaS Part 1: Enterprise SSO Readiness: SAML vs OIDC for B2B SaaS Part 2: Validating SAML Responses: Signatures, Audience & Clock Skew Part 3: SCIM Provisioning & Deprovisioning That Actually Removes Access Part 4: Multi-Tenant Login Routing: Domain Discovery & Enforced SSO Part 5: Just-in-Time Provisioning & Role Mapping From IdP Groups Part 6 (This Post): Break-Glass Accounts & SSO Audit Logs Related earlier posts: Step-Up Authentication for Sensitive Actions · Session Lifecycle Hardening: Rotation, Timeouts & Server-Side Revocation What break-glass is, and what it is not Break-glass is a deliberately inconvenient emergency door. It is not a second normal login. The design goals: It works when the IdP, the SAML certificate or the OIDC discovery endpoint is broken. Only a named, tiny set of people per tenant can use it. Every use is loud: alerts, audit entries and a short session. It cannot become the everyday path that quietly defeats enforced SSO. Three ways to provide emergency access Approach How it works Pros Risks Tenant break-glass user 1–2 local accounts per tenant, password + hardware key, exempt from SSO enforcement Customer stays in control; works offline from IdP Credentials forgotten or shared; must be tested Vendor-assisted bypass Your support temporarily disables enforcement after verified request No standing credentials Social-engineering target; slow at 3 a.m. Secondary IdP connection Backup SAML/OIDC connection to another IdP Still SSO Rarely set up; same misconfig risk In practice I ship the first option as the default and keep the second as a documented, heavily verified fallback. The secondary connection is nice for very large customers, but almost nobody maintains it. Modelling it in the database I keep break-glass status as an explicit flag on the membership, never as "user has a password set", because JIT and SCIM users sometimes end up with passwords from old flows. ALTER TABLE tenant_memberships ADD COLUMN break_glass boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false , ADD COLUMN break_glass_last_used_at timestamptz , ADD COLUMN break_glass_last_tested_at timestamptz ; -- At most two break-glass members per tenant CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_or_two_break_glass ON tenant_memberships ( tenant_id , break_glass_slot ) WHERE break_glass = true ; ~~~ { % endraw % } The { % raw % } `break_glass_slot` { % endraw % } column is 1 or 2 , which gives a hard limit without a trigger . ## The login rule Enforced SSO blocks password login for everyone except flagged break - glass members , and those members must use a phishing - resistant factor : { % raw % } ~~~ php public function canUsePasswordLogin ( Membership $m ) : bool { if ( ! $m -> tenant -> sso_enforced ) { return true ; } return $m -> break_glass && $m -> user -> hasWebAuthnCredential ( ) ; // hardware key or platform passkey only } public function afterBreakGlassLogin ( Membership $m , Request $request ) : void { $m -> forceFill ( [ 'break_glass_last_used_at' => now ( ) ] ) -> save ( ) ; session ( ) -> put ( 'max_lifetime_minutes' , 60 ) ; // short session, no remember-me AuditLog :: record ( 'auth.break_glass.used' , $m , $request , severity : 'critical' ) ; Notification :: send ( $m -> tenant -> securityContacts ( ) , new BreakGlassUsed ( $m ) ) ; } ~~~ { % endraw % } Three details matter . No SMS or email codes for this account : they are the weakest factors and the exact thing an attacker targets . No remember - me cookie . And the alert goes to the tenant 's security contacts, not only to the person logging in. ## Testing it before you need it An untested break-glass account is a password nobody remembers. I nudge tenant admins to test quarterly and record the result in {% raw %}`break_glass_last_tested_at`. In the admin UI, a tenant with enforced SSO and no successful test in 90 days gets a visible warning. For timestamps in alerts and support tickets, I keep everything in UTC; when someone sends a Unix time from a log line, a quick [Unix timestamp converter](https://pixelvalut.com/tools/unix-timestamp-converter?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=break-glass-accounts-sso-audit-logs) avoids off-by-five-hours mistakes across time zones. ## What to log for every SSO event Most SSO incidents I have debugged were slow because the logs said "login failed" and nothing else. This is the shape I use: ~~~json { "ts": "2026-11-22T07:14:03.512Z", "event": "auth.sso.failed", "tenant_id": "t_8f21", "connection_id": "saml_okta_01", "subject": "00u1a2b3c4", "email_domain": "example.com", "reason": "audience_mismatch", "detail": "expected https://app.example.io/saml/t_8f21", "ip": "203.0.113.24", "user_agent_hash": "9c1f...", "request_id": "req_71b9", "prev_hash": "4e07...", "hash": "b2d9..." } ~~~ Things I deliberately include: a machine-readable `reason` from a fixed list (signature_invalid, audience_mismatch, clock_skew, unknown_connection, user_deprovisioned), the connection ID, and the request ID that ties the log to traces. Things I deliberately leave out: the raw SAML assertion, ID tokens, and full email addresses in high-volume logs. Domain is usually enough for debugging, and tokens in logs are a breach waiting to happen. The events I always record: - SSO login success and failure, with reason - Break-glass login, failed break-glass attempt, and break-glass flag changes - Enforcement turned on or off, and by whom - SAML certificate or OIDC client secret rotated - Group-to-role mapping edits (from Part 5) - SCIM deactivation and reactivation (from Part 3) ## Making logs tamper-evident An attacker who gets admin access will try to clean up after themselves. A simple hash chain makes deletion or editing visible. Each entry stores the hash of the previous one: ~~~php $prev = AuditLog::where(' tenant_id ', $tenantId)->latest(' id ')->value(' hash ') ?? str_repeat(' 0 ', 64); $payload = json_encode($entry, JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES); $entry[' prev_hash '] = $prev; $entry[' hash '] = hash(' sha256 ', $prev . $payload); ~~~ A nightly job walks each tenant' s chain and alerts on a break . For extra safety , ship a daily digest of the last hash to a separate write - once bucket . When I want to check a value by hand during a review , the [ hash generator ] ( https : //pixelvalut.com/tools/hash-generator?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=break-glass-accounts-sso-audit-logs) on PixelValut is a quick way to confirm a SHA-256 of a known payload. Quick answer: A break-glass account is a tightly limited local login that still works when a tenant's SSO fails. Keep one or two per tenant, protect them with a hardware-key MFA factor, alert on every use, and expire their sessions fast. Log every SSO event with tenant, subject, result and reason, in UTC, hash-chained so tampering shows.

Enforced SSO is the goal of most enterprise deals. Then one morning the customer's certificate rotates, or their Entra ID tenant has an outage, or an admin deletes the app assignment by mistake, and 400 people cannot reach your product. If enforced SSO means there is no other way in, you now have a support incident you cannot fix from your side without bypassing your own security.

Break-glass access and good audit logs are the two pieces that make enforced SSO safe to sell. This last part of the series covers both. I wrote it with help from AI tools and checked it against NIST SP 800-63B guidance on authenticators and the Okta and Microsoft Entra ID documentation on emergency access accounts. Everything here is defensive design for your own application.

📚 Series Navigation — Enterprise SSO & Identity for B2B SaaS

  • Part 1: Enterprise SSO Readiness: SAML vs OIDC for B2B SaaS
  • Part 2: Validating SAML Responses: Signatures, Audience & Clock Skew
  • Part 3: SCIM Provisioning & Deprovisioning That Actually Removes Access
  • Part 4: Multi-Tenant Login Routing: Domain Discovery & Enforced SSO
  • Part 5: Just-in-Time Provisioning & Role Mapping From IdP Groups
  • Part 6 (This Post): Break-Glass Accounts & SSO Audit Logs

Related earlier posts: Step-Up Authentication for Sensitive Actions · Session Lifecycle Hardening: Rotation, Timeouts & Server-Side Revocation

What break-glass is, and what it is not

Break-glass is a deliberately inconvenient emergency door. It is not a second normal login. The design goals:

  • It works when the IdP, the SAML certificate or the OIDC discovery endpoint is broken.
  • Only a named, tiny set of people per tenant can use it.
  • Every use is loud: alerts, audit entries and a short session.
  • It cannot become the everyday path that quietly defeats enforced SSO.
Three ways to provide emergency access
Approach How it works Pros Risks Tenant break-glass user 1–2 local accounts per tenant, password + hardware key, exempt from SSO enforcement Customer stays in control; works offline from IdP Credentials forgotten or shared; must be tested Vendor-assisted bypass Your support temporarily disables enforcement after verified request No standing credentials Social-engineering target; slow at 3 a.m. Secondary IdP connection Backup SAML/OIDC connection to another IdP Still SSO Rarely set up; same misconfig risk

In practice I ship the first option as the default and keep the second as a documented, heavily verified fallback. The secondary connection is nice for very large customers, but almost nobody maintains it.

Modelling it in the database

I keep break-glass status as an explicit flag on the membership, never as "user has a password set", because JIT and SCIM users sometimes end up with passwords from old flows.

ALTER TABLE tenant_memberships
  ADD COLUMN break_glass boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  ADD COLUMN break_glass_last_used_at timestamptz,
  ADD COLUMN break_glass_last_tested_at timestamptz;

-- At most two break-glass members per tenant
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_or_two_break_glass
  ON tenant_memberships (tenant_id, break_glass_slot)
  WHERE break_glass = true;
~~~{% endraw %}

The {% raw %}`break_glass_slot`{% endraw %} column is 1 or 2, which gives a hard limit without a trigger.

## The login rule

Enforced SSO blocks password login for everyone except flagged break-glass members, and those members must use a phishing-resistant factor:{% raw %}

~~~php
public function canUsePasswordLogin(Membership $m): bool
{
    if (! $m->tenant->sso_enforced) {
        return true;
    }

    return $m->break_glass
        && $m->user->hasWebAuthnCredential(); // hardware key or platform passkey only
}

public function afterBreakGlassLogin(Membership $m, Request $request): void
{
    $m->forceFill(['break_glass_last_used_at' => now()])->save();

    session()->put('max_lifetime_minutes', 60);   // short session, no remember-me
    AuditLog::record('auth.break_glass.used', $m, $request, severity: 'critical');
    Notification::send($m->tenant->securityContacts(), new BreakGlassUsed($m));
}
~~~{% endraw %}

Three details matter. No SMS or email codes for this account: they are the weakest factors and the exact thing an attacker targets. No remember-me cookie. And the alert goes to the tenant's security contacts, not only to the person logging in.

## Testing it before you need it

An untested break-glass account is a password nobody remembers. I nudge tenant admins to test quarterly and record the result in {% raw %}`break_glass_last_tested_at`. In the admin UI, a tenant with enforced SSO and no successful test in 90 days gets a visible warning. For timestamps in alerts and support tickets, I keep everything in UTC; when someone sends a Unix time from a log line, a quick [Unix timestamp converter](https://pixelvalut.com/tools/unix-timestamp-converter?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=break-glass-accounts-sso-audit-logs) avoids off-by-five-hours mistakes across time zones.

## What to log for every SSO event

Most SSO incidents I have debugged were slow because the logs said "login failed" and nothing else. This is the shape I use:

~~~json
{
  "ts": "2026-11-22T07:14:03.512Z",
  "event": "auth.sso.failed",
  "tenant_id": "t_8f21",
  "connection_id": "saml_okta_01",
  "subject": "00u1a2b3c4",
  "email_domain": "example.com",
  "reason": "audience_mismatch",
  "detail": "expected https://app.example.io/saml/t_8f21",
  "ip": "203.0.113.24",
  "user_agent_hash": "9c1f...",
  "request_id": "req_71b9",
  "prev_hash": "4e07...",
  "hash": "b2d9..."
}
~~~

Things I deliberately include: a machine-readable `reason` from a fixed list (signature_invalid, audience_mismatch, clock_skew, unknown_connection, user_deprovisioned), the connection ID, and the request ID that ties the log to traces. Things I deliberately leave out: the raw SAML assertion, ID tokens, and full email addresses in high-volume logs. Domain is usually enough for debugging, and tokens in logs are a breach waiting to happen.

The events I always record:

- SSO login success and failure, with reason
- Break-glass login, failed break-glass attempt, and break-glass flag changes
- Enforcement turned on or off, and by whom
- SAML certificate or OIDC client secret rotated
- Group-to-role mapping edits (from Part 5)
- SCIM deactivation and reactivation (from Part 3)

## Making logs tamper-evident

An attacker who gets admin access will try to clean up after themselves. A simple hash chain makes deletion or editing visible. Each entry stores the hash of the previous one:

~~~php
$prev = AuditLog::where('tenant_id', $tenantId)->latest('id')->value('hash') ?? str_repeat('0', 64);
$payload = json_encode($entry, JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES);
$entry['prev_hash'] = $prev;
$entry['hash'] = hash('sha256', $prev . $payload);
~~~

A nightly job walks each tenant's chain and alerts on a break. For extra safety, ship a daily digest of the last hash to a separate write-once bucket. When I want to check a value by hand during a review, the [hash generator](https://pixelvalut.com/tools/hash-generator?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=break-glass-accounts-sso-audit-logs) on PixelValut is a quick way to confirm a SHA-256 of a known payload.

This is not a replacement for a proper append-only store or a SIEM. It is a cheap layer that makes "someone deleted the evidence" detectable.

## Giving customers their own logs

Enterprise buyers will ask for audit log export in security reviews. Offer a filtered view in the admin UI, a CSV/JSON export, and, for larger plans, a streaming option to their SIEM through a webhook or S3 delivery. Keep at least 12 months of retention for auth events; many customer questionnaires ask for it.

## Diagnostic checklist

- [ ] Each SSO-enforced tenant has 1–2 break-glass members, no more
- [ ] Break-glass login requires a WebAuthn factor, no SMS or email OTP
- [ ] Break-glass sessions are short and have no remember-me
- [ ] Every break-glass use alerts the tenant's security contacts
- [ ] Untested break-glass accounts (90+ days) show a warning
- [ ] SSO failures log a fixed reason code and connection ID
- [ ] Raw assertions and tokens are never written to logs
- [ ] Audit entries are hash-chained and verified nightly
- [ ] Customers can export or stream their auth logs

## FAQ

### Doesn't a break-glass account defeat the point of enforced SSO?
Only if it is easy and quiet. Limiting it to two people, requiring a hardware key, alerting on every use and keeping sessions short keeps it an emergency path, not a back door.

### Who should own the break-glass accounts, us or the customer?
The customer. Your staff should not hold standing credentials into customer tenants. Your fallback is a verified support process, not a password.

Twelve months is a common minimum in enterprise questionnaires. Some regulated customers ask for longer; make retention a per-plan setting.

### Should failed logins include the email address?
In the tenant's own audit view, it is useful. In high-volume platform logs, prefer the domain or a hashed identifier to limit personal data exposure.

### Is a hash chain enough to prove logs were not changed?
It proves the chain is internally consistent. Pair it with a daily anchor stored somewhere the application cannot overwrite, and an external SIEM for high-value tenants.

A small honest number beats a big vague claim. ### Should I update my resume if I am happy in my job? Yes. A ready resume is also useful for promotions, internal transfers and conference bios. It is not a signal that you plan to leave. ### Where should I store these files? Anywhere you control that survives losing your work laptop: a personal cloud drive or a private Git repo on your own account. Not on company systems. ### How do I keep the habit going? Put a 5-minute Friday calendar block and a 20-minute first-Monday-of-the-month block on your personal calendar. Every quarter I export the master to a clean one-column PDF and DOCX and run it through a parser, because templates and fonts drift and you only notice when a portal mangles your dates. I use the [ATS resume checker](https://smartresumeanalyzer.com/ats-resume-checker?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=resume-always-ready) on Smart Resume Analyzer for this, then run one real job description through [resume vs job match](https://smartresumeanalyzer.com/resume-job-match?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=resume-always-ready) to see which keywords I am missing for the roles I would want next.

What I look for:

- Job titles, company names and dates land in the right fields.
- No skills hidden in headers, footers, text boxes or images.
- Section names are standard: Experience, Skills, Education, Projects.
- The top third answers "what level and what kind of engineer" in one line.

## Keeping LinkedIn in sync

Recruiters search LinkedIn long before you apply anywhere. If your profile still says the job you had three years ago, you are invisible to the searches that matter. Quarterly, I copy the headline and top three wins from the master into LinkedIn. The [LinkedIn optimizer](https://smartresumeanalyzer.com/tools/linkedin-optimizer?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=resume-always-ready) is handy for spotting a weak headline or an About section with no searchable terms.

A note on "Open to work": you can turn on the recruiter-only version without telling your network. That is a personal call. A ready profile works either way.

## Ready resume vs panic resume

| Signal | Panic resume (day 1 of layoff) | Ready resume (maintained) |
|---|---|---|
| Numbers | Guessed or missing | Recorded when they happened |
| Most recent role | Thin, written last | Richest section |
| Time to first application | 7–14 days | 1–2 days |
| Tailoring per job | Rewrite from scratch | Copy master, cut, reorder |
| ATS formatting | Unknown until rejected | Checked last quarter |
| Stress | High | Still high, but you are moving |

## What to keep when you leave suddenly

Layoffs often cut access the same hour. If your notes live only in company Confluence or Slack, they are gone. Things that are fine and smart to keep in your own space, written by you, with nothing confidential:

- Your own brag notes and review self-assessments.
- Public links: blog posts, conference talks, open source PRs, app store pages.
- Names and personal contact details of colleagues willing to be references (ask them first).
- Your offer letter, pay slips and equity documents, which you are entitled to.

Things not to take: source code, internal documents, customer data or anything under NDA. Describe the outcome in your own words instead.

## The diagnostic checklist

Run this today. If you tick fewer than six, you are not ready yet.

- [ ] I have a private brag file outside employer systems
- [ ] It has an entry from the last 14 days
- [ ] My master resume mentions my current role with at least 4 numbered bullets
- [ ] My skills section lists tools I used in the last 12 months
- [ ] I ran an ATS parse check in the last 3 months
- [ ] My LinkedIn headline matches the level I want next
- [ ] I know which 2–3 people would give a reference, and they know too
- [ ] I could send a tailored application within 48 hours

## FAQ

### How long should the master resume be?
As long as it needs to be. Mine is around three pages. The version you send is one to two pages, cut from the master for each role.

### Is a brag document the same as a performance self-review?
They feed each other. The brag file is raw and weekly. The self-review is a summary twice a year. Writing the brag file makes the review take an hour instead of a weekend.

### What if my wins are hard to measure?
Use time, scope or people instead of money: "cut onboarding from 3 weeks to 1", "owned 4 services", "unblocked 2 teams". A small honest number beats a big vague claim.

### Should I update my resume if I am happy in my job?
Yes. A ready resume is also useful for promotions, internal transfers and conference bios. It is not a signal that you plan to leave.

### Where should I store these files?
Anywhere you control that survives losing your work laptop: a personal cloud drive or a private Git repo on your own account. Not on company systems.

### How do I keep the habit going?
Put a 5-minute Friday calendar block and a 20-minute first-Monday-of-the-month block on your personal calendar. Small and boring is the point.

## Wrapping up the series

Layoffs, gaps, comebacks, choppy timelines and track changes are all easier when the evidence already exists. That is the whole series in one line: write it down while it is true. If you want a quick check of where your current resume stands, start with the [Smart Resume Analyzer ATS checker](https://smartresumeanalyzer.com/ats-resume-checker?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=series&utm_campaign=resume-always-ready).

Most engineering teams building multilingual products treat localization as a content problem handled by "someone else." Then the day comes when you switch translation vendors, or bring localization in-house, and discover that years of translated strings, context, and terminology decisions live locked inside a third-party CAT tool with no clean export path.

This is the same underlying issue described in this piece on translation memories and glossaries as corporate assets, but from a business/ownership angle. I want to cover the technical side: how to actually manage these assets as versioned, portable data instead of vendor lock-in, and how to wire them into your i18n pipeline.

TM and glossary data are just structured data

Strip away the terminology and you have two artifacts:

  • Translation Memory (TM): a set of aligned source/target segment pairs, usually with metadata (date, project, match quality). Standard interchange format is TMX (Translation Memory eXchange, XML-based).
  • Glossary / Termbase: a curated key-term list with approved translations per locale, often with part-of-speech, domain, and usage notes. Standard format is TBX (TermBase eXchange), though plenty of teams just use CSV/XLSX.

Both are portable, machine-readable, and version-controllable. There's no technical reason they should live exclusively inside a vendor's proprietary system.

A minimal pipeline for owning your linguistic assets

Here's a setup that works whether you're using a CAT tool, an LLM-based translation workflow, or both.

1. Treat your glossary as a config file, not a spreadsheet buried in Drive 
{
  "term": "invoice",
  "domain": "finance",
  "translations": {
    "pt-PT": "fatura",
    "pt-BR": "nota fiscal",
    "es-ES": "factura",
    "fr-FR": "facture"
  },
  "do_not_translate": false,
  "notes": "pt-BR uses different legal term than pt-PT, not interchangeable"
}

Put this in a repo. Review changes via pull request, the same way you'd review a schema migration. Legal, product, and marketing can comment on the diff instead of emailing a spreadsheet around.

2. Export TMs in TMX and store them, don't let them live only in the vendor's cloud

Any competent CAT tool (memoQ, Trados, Phrase, Smartling) supports TMX export. Automate this:

# Pseudocode for a nightly TM export job
curl -X GET "https://api.vendor.com/v1/tm/export?format=tmx" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VENDOR_API_KEY" \
  -o "tm_backup_$(date +%F).tmx"

aws s3 cp "tm_backup_$(date +%F).tmx" s3://your-bucket/translation-memories/

This single script solves the "vendor lock-in" problem the source article describes from a legal/ownership angle. If you own a daily TMX snapshot, switching suppliers costs you a re-import, not a rebuild.

3. Feed TM and glossary into your translation pipeline automatically

If you're using machine translation or LLMs as part of a hybrid workflow, the glossary should be injected into the prompt or the API call, not applied as a post-hoc find-and-replace.

import json

def build_translation_prompt(source_text, target_locale, glossary_path="glossary.json"):
    with open(glossary_path) as f:
        glossary = json.load(f)

    relevant_terms = [
        f"{entry['term']} -> {entry['translations'][target_locale]}"
        for entry in glossary
        if target_locale in entry['translations']
    ]

    prompt = f"""Translate the following text to {target_locale}.
Use these approved terms exactly as specified, do not deviate:
{chr(10).join(relevant_terms)}

Text:
{source_text}
"""
    return prompt

For API-based MT providers (DeepL, Google Cloud Translation, Azure Translator), check if they support glossary upload natively:

  • DeepL API supports glossaries via POST /v2/glossaries, scoped per language pair.
  • Google Cloud Translation supports glossaries as a resource you reference in translate requests.
  • Azure Translator supports "Custom Translator" with phrase dictionaries.

Using the native glossary feature is almost always better than prompt injection because it's deterministic, not probabilistic.

4. Validate TM matches before accepting them

Not all 100% matches are safe to reuse blindly, context can shift meaning. A lightweight validation step:

def is_safe_reuse(segment, tm_match, min_confidence=0.95):
    if tm_match['match_score'] < min_confidence:
        return False
    if tm_match['domain'] != segment.get('domain'):
        return False  # same string, different context, flag for review
    return True

This matters more than it sounds. A term like "charge" translates differently in a billing context versus a battery/hardware context. A naive 100%-match TM reuse will silently propagate the wrong one across your whole product.

Quality tiers, as a CI concept

The source article mentions defining quality tiers by document type: contracts need stricter review than internal reports. You can model this directly in your localization CI:

# l10n-config.yml
tiers:
  legal:
    tm_write: false        # don't pollute the core TM with ad hoc legal translations
    glossary_enforced: strict
    human_review: required
  marketing:
    tm_write: true
    glossary_enforced: moderate
    human_review: optional
  internal_docs:
    tm_write: false
    glossary_enforced: none
    human_review: none

Gate your pipeline on this config so low-rigor translations never get auto-merged into the assets that feed high-stakes documents.

Why this is worth the setup cost

Engineering teams are usually the ones who feel the pain first when linguistic assets are mismanaged: inconsistent strings across locales, repeated translation costs for identical UI copy, broken terminology after a vendor switch. The fix isn't exotic. It's the same discipline applied to any other data asset: standard formats, version control, automated export, and validation gates.

If you're setting this up for the first time, start small: export your current TM to TMX today, put your glossary in a JSON or YAML file in a repo, and automate the nightly backup. Everything else builds on that foundation.

items.title: High-Altitude Wind Load Dynamics in Vertical Robotics: Gust Compensation and Dew-Point Telemetry
items.summary: Operating a robotic cleaner on an interior glass partition is a predictable mechanical task. Deploying the same device on the exterior facade of a 30-story building introduces violent aerodynamic variables. At high altitudes, wind shear, sudden pressure gusts, and rapid surface condensation can compromise vacuum adhesion within milliseconds. To prevent wind-induced detachment on exterior glazing, modern vertical platforms integrate real-time atmospheric telemetry with closed-loop turbine modulation. Here is how exterior vertical robotics detect environmental hazards and compensate for external wind loads. Aerodynamic Peeling Forces and Bernoulli Suction Losses When high-velocity wind sweeps across a vertical building facade, it creates localized low-pressure zones governed by the Bernoulli principle. This external airflow actively pulls against the robot chassis, generating a peeling torque that attempts to lift the windward edge of the silicone sealing skirt. To counteract external wind pressure without draining battery reserves during calm conditions, modern controllers implement dynamic suction scaling: Internal differential pressure transducers sample chamber vacuum levels at 500 Hz. When a wind gust causes a sudden 150-Pascal fluctuation in internal chamber pressure, the firmware immediately ramps the brushless centrifugal impeller from its nominal 20,000 RPM eco-cruise speed up to its peak 26,000 RPM hold threshold. Once ambient pressure stabilizes for more than 10 seconds, the controller steps down turbine power to conserve thermal headroom. Capacitive Rain and Dew-Point Detection Surface moisture outside a building behaves very differently from controlled ultrasonic spray mist. Sudden rain showers or morning condensation drop the glass friction coefficient below 0.15, causing drive tracks to hydroplane and slide uncontrollably downward. Because optical sensors often confuse water droplets with glass reflections, exterior-rated robotics rely on dedicated environmental arrays: Interdigitated capacitive moisture grids mounted along the top leading edge of the chassis detect conductive water droplets before the drive wheels make contact. Onboard ambient temperature and relative humidity sensors continuously calculate the local dew point. If the glass surface temperature approaches the dew point threshold, the system suspends spray cycles and initiates an automated return-to-origin sequence. Structural Glass Flexion and Track Suspension Compliance Large exterior architectural panes are not completely rigid; under strong wind loads, double-glazed Insulated Glass Units (IGUs) bow inward and outward by several millimeters. A rigid chassis crossing a flexing glass surface experiences uneven seal compression, leading to micro-leaks. Hardware engineers solve this through articulated suspension kinematics: Independent spring-loaded drive track assemblies maintain 4 to 6 millimeters of vertical travel, allowing the tracks to conform to curved or bowing glass panes while keeping the central vacuum plenum flat. Dual-lip thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) skirts flex dynamically to maintain an airtight seal across uneven glazing deflections. Empirical Outdoor Testing and Lab Benchmarks Validating exterior safety algorithms requires controlled wind-tunnel simulations and multi-story facade testing rather than simple indoor bench runs. Key empirical metrics include: Maximum lateral wind speed tolerance before vacuum seal degradation occurs. Response latency between sudden moisture detection and emergency path abortion. Drive track traction retention across wet versus dry tempered glass under simulated wind gusts. For comprehensive hardware teardowns, exterior wind-load endurance charts, and comparative safety evaluations across commercial vertical robotics, review the empirical laboratory reports published at Best Window Cleaning Robot Have you designed outdoor robotics or embedded weather-compensated control loops? What sensor combinations have proven most reliable for detecting sudden moisture and wind shear in field deployments? Share your engineering insights in the comments below.

items.title: A small test fixture for Chinese SRT subtitle imports
items.summary: A subtitle import problem is easier to isolate with a tiny fixture than with a full video transcript. This example separates three checks: whether the editor can decode Chinese characters, parse cue timing, and keep line breaks. It is a proposed diagnostic fixture, not a report of tests across editing applications. Start with two cues Save the following as a UTF-8 text file with an .srt extension: 1 00:00:01,000 --> 00:00:04,000 简体中文测试：你好，世界。 2 00:00:05,000 --> 00:00:08,000 繁體中文測試：你好，世界。 第二行字幕。 The wording is deliberately simple. It is sample text for testing display, not a translation of any real recording. Diagnose one thing at a time Garbled characters: reopen the file in a text editor and check its encoding. If the saved file already contains replacement characters, choosing a different font cannot recover the lost text; return to the original export. If the text file is readable but the video editor shows empty boxes, investigate the selected subtitle font and its Chinese glyph coverage. No subtitles: confirm that the importer expects a subtitle file rather than a video file or plain transcript. Check the extension, the comma before milliseconds, the arrow between timestamps, and the blank line between cues. Unexpected timing: the first cue should begin one second into the timeline and end at four seconds. The second should start at five seconds and end at eight. Place the test on a matching timeline before diagnosing a full export that may have an offset. A constant offset and progressively increasing drift are different problems; do not fix both by shifting every cue by the same amount. Unexpected wrapping: the second cue deliberately contains a line break. Check it at the intended video resolution, not just in the text editor. Line length alone does not tell you whether a subtitle is comfortable to read: font size, display duration, and the surrounding image also matter. Replace the fixture with the real translation Once the fixture imports correctly, test a short segment of the actual translated subtitles. Review names, numbers, and sentence boundaries against the original audio. A technically valid SRT file can still contain an inaccurate translation. Keep a copy of the original subtitle export before changing timestamps or converting character sets. items.summary: Everyone’s impressed by what AI can do. Here’s how a model actually works, and why running one takes GPUs that cost more than a car. What Happens When You Send a Prompt Every time you send a prompt to a language model, whether small, medium or large, you make an API call from a device and get an answer back in seconds. It feels instant, but behind the scenes a lot of work happens to produce that answer. Every model also has limits it must work within. The most common ones are: Capacity limits: The model can only read and respond within a fixed token limit. Knowledge limits: The model only knows what was in its training data, up to its cutoff date. Behavioral limits: Safety training, usage policies, system prompts and guardrails decide what it will and won’t do. Governance limits: Data privacy and residency rules, regulations, and audit and observability requirements decide how and where it can operate. Start Simple: A Very Basic Model Imagine a very small machine. You give it an input, and it always gives you the same output for that input. This machine takes any number X, adds 5 to it every time, and returns X + 5. Give it 10, and you get 15. Give it 100, and you get 105. Simple machine In LLM terms: X is your prompt (the input). 5 is the model parameter: what the machine has “learned.” X + 5 is the model’s response (the output). Making the Model a Little Smarter Now let’s make our machine a little smarter. Instead of just adding a number, it multiplies the input by one value and adds another: Output = (w × X) + b Simple model Here w (weight) and b (bias) aren’t chosen by us. The machine learns them by looking at thousands of examples. Weight (w) controls how much influence the input has on the output. Bias (b) is the model’s built-in starting point before it considers the input. In fact, our first machine was this same formula with w = 1 and b = 5. Weight and Bias in the Housing Market Weight decides how much an input affects the price: Large weight: a small change in the input causes a big change in the output. Near-zero weight: the input hardly matters. Negative weight: the output goes down as the input goes up. For example, if w = 2,000, every extra square foot adds ₹2,000 to the price. If the model learns a negative weight for “age of house,” older houses get cheaper. Bias is the starting point: the output you get before any input is counted. It’s a fixed amount added at the end. For example, if b = ₹1,00,000, the house has a base value of ₹1 lakh before its size is even considered. You can think of it as the value of the land or a market baseline. So a 1,000 sq ft flat would be priced at: (2,000 × 1,000) + 1,00,000 = ₹21,00,000 (₹21 lakh) Putting them together, imagine a line on a graph: The weight sets how steep the line is (the slope). The bias sets where the line starts (the intercept, the point where it crosses the vertical axis). Training is just the machine trying different slopes and starting points until the line fits the data best. Our two machines side by side: The +5 machine: w = 1, b = 5. It passes the input through unchanged and adds 5. The house-price machine: w = 2,000, b = ₹1,00,000. It charges ₹2,000 per sq ft, starting from ₹1 lakh. Table 1 From Two Parameters to Billions Our house-price model has just two parameters. A real house price depends on much more: location, floor, number of bedrooms, distance to the metro, the builder’s reputation. Each new factor brings its own weight. Stack thousands of these small machines in layers, with each layer passing its output to the next, and you get a neural network. An LLM is the same idea at a huge scale. Its input isn’t square footage but your prompt, broken into tokens. Its output isn’t a price but the most likely next word. And its parameters don’t number two. They number in the billions, each one a weight or bias learned from huge amounts of text. No single weight “knows” anything. Just as no single factor sets the price of a flat in Mumbai, the intelligence comes from billions of them working together. And all those billions have to live somewhere. A 70-billion-parameter model needs about 140 GB of memory just to hold its weights, before it answers a single question. Every time you make an API call, those weights, already loaded on GPUs, are multiplied against your prompt, and the result is sent back to you as an answer in seconds, for thousands of people at once. A model’s knowledge lives in its weights. But billions of weights are useless if there’s nowhere fast enough to run them. So where do those 140 GB (70 billion weights at the standard 2 bytes each) actually live? What does the work when you send a request? And why do the GPUs behind it cost more than a car? Let’s find out, starting with some basics. Transformers: How the Model Thinks Our house-price example needed only a handful of weights. Today’s models can summarize a 100-page document. To make that possible, the weights grow into the billions and the model grows into many layers stacked on top of each other. The output of one layer becomes the input to the next. Simple network This entire network of layers is called a transformer. What makes it special is a mechanism called attention: at every layer, each word looks at the other words in the input to work out which ones matter most for its meaning. In simple terms, the transformer is the formula (like the house-price calculator from earlier). It’s written once in code and is broadly the same across GPT, Llama and Claude. What makes them different is not the formula; it’s the weights (like the price per square foot). Transformer The formula (the transformer) is only a few pages of code; the knowledge is in the weights. A real model doesn’t have one or two weights; it has billions of them. These billions of weights are what training produces, and together they can take up tens or even hundreds of GB. They are simply files sitting on a disk, and their size varies from model to model. Before the model can answer a single request, all of its weights have to be loaded into memory. One may ask: why can’t a large model run well on a personal computer or a small server? To understand, let’s look at how a normal laptop or server performs a calculation. Why a Large Model Doesn’t Fit in a Laptop: CPU and RAM You open the calculator on your laptop and calculate 100 × 2. What happens? The calculator responds with 200. Behind the scenes, the CPU and RAM are doing all the work. See the diagram below. Simple CPU-RAM When you ask it to calculate 100 × 2, this is how it works: the computer saves the instructions in RAM, the CPU fetches the instructions from RAM, computes the result, and saves it back to RAM. Here the CPU is doing all the work, while RAM acts as temporary storage, holding the instructions and data the CPU is currently working on. This setup has three limits when it comes to running a large model: 1. A normal laptop has a limited number of CPU cores. The latest Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors offer 6, 8, 12 or 16 cores, so a laptop can process only a small number of calculations in parallel, compared with the thousands of cores in a GPU. 2. A typical laptop has 16–32 GB of RAM, whereas a rack server may have 512 GB or more, but the weights of the largest models can go beyond even that. 3. Data moves between the CPU and RAM over a fairly narrow channel: roughly 77–128 GB/s on a laptop, and a few hundred GB/s on a large server. That sounds fast, but a model has to read all of its weights for every word it generates. Even if a 140 GB model fit in a laptop’s memory, at 100 GB/s it would take more than a second per word. Where the Model Lives and Works: GPU and VRAM To run a large model quickly, we need three things: thousands of cores working in parallel, hundreds of GB of memory, and a very fast link between the two. Get all three, and the LLM can answer our requests much faster. That’s exactly what NVIDIA’s GPUs and their VRAM provide, solving each of the problems we discussed earlier. 1. Parallel processing: A basic or entry-level modern NVIDIA GPU typically has around 2,560 to 3,840 CUDA cores (such as the GeForce RTX 5050 with 2,560 CUDA cores and RTX 5060 with 3,840 CUDA cores), while high-end models reach 10,000 to over 21,000. Each CUDA core is far simpler than a CPU core, but together they can do thousands of small calculations at once, which is exactly what a model needs. 2. Memory capacity: A basic or entry-level modern NVIDIA GPU typically comes with 8 GB of VRAM (such as the GeForce RTX 5050 and RTX 5060), while mid-range models offer 12 GB to 16 GB and flagship cards reach 32 GB (RTX 5090). That’s still far short of 140 GB, which is why serious models run on data-center GPUs such as the H100 (80 GB) or B200 (192 GB), often several linked together. 3. Memory bandwidth: Data transfer between a GPU chip and its VRAM typically ranges from 320 GB/s on entry-level cards to 1,792 GB/s on flagship gaming GPUs, and reaches 3,000–8,000 GB/s on data-center GPUs. GPU Unlike the CPU and RAM, the GPU and its VRAM sit on the same card (on data-center GPUs, the same chip package), connected by a much wider channel. That is what lets data move at such high speed. The table below compares cores and memory (source: Intel and NVIDIA websites). Table 2 Who Drives It: Software and Model Servers A chip on its own can’t do anything useful; something needs to drive it. That’s where software comes in: CUDA, NVIDIA’s platform for programming its GPUs, and PyTorch, the popular framework built on top of it that most AI models are written in. With a few lines of PyTorch code, you can load a model, ask it a question and get an answer. A very small model can even run this way on your laptop. In production, though, it’s not just one request: many users can send requests at the same time. So we need something that keeps listening for requests and serves them around the clock. That’s where a model server such as vLLM comes into the picture. vLLM is built on PyTorch; it wraps the model in a service, exposes an HTTP endpoint (an address apps can send requests to), and batches requests from many users together so the GPU stays busy. A Closer Look at a Model Server When a model server starts, it loads all the weights into VRAM once. After that, the server stays up and waits for requests. At its core, the model is a prediction machine: given your input, it predicts the next word. More precisely, it works on tokens, which are words or pieces of words. For each new token, it looks at all the tokens so far (your prompt plus everything it has written) and predicts the next one. It repeats this loop until it predicts a special end token or reaches a length limit. Because the answer is produced one token at a time and sent back as each token is generated, ChatGPT’s reply appears word by word. A Closer Look at the Token Prediction Loop When you send a big prompt to ChatGPT, there’s a short delay, and then the answer streams out steadily. The delay is called the prefill step, and the streaming is called the decode (or streaming) step. Fig 1 The loop has two parts: 1. The prefill step: when you ask a question, your prompt is first converted into tokens. The GPU then processes all of these tokens together, in parallel, in a single pass through the model. Along the way, it saves its intermediate results for each token (called the KV cache) so it never has to redo it. So whether you send 20 tokens or 2,000, the weights are read from VRAM only about once. A longer prompt just means more calculation, which is why a big prompt causes a longer delay. Once the first token is generated, the answer starts appearing on your screen. The time this takes is called TTFT (time to first token). 2. The streaming step: from here, the model produces one token at a time. For every new token, the GPU has to read all of the weights from VRAM again, so this step’s speed is limited by memory bandwidth, not by the number of cores. That’s why the answer streams out at a steady pace, and why fast VRAM matters so much. The delay between two output tokens is called TPOT (time per output token). TTFT and TPOT are the two basic benchmarks for any LLM serving setup. They depend on the GPU, but also on the model’s size and the model server running it. Prefill speed (TTFT) depends mostly on the GPU’s compute power, while streaming speed (TPOT) depends mostly on its memory bandwidth. A Closer Look at Caching The KV cache works well within a single request. However, once the model has responded, the cache is normally cleared, and the model remembers nothing. So the chat app keeps track of the history and sends the entire conversation to the model every time the user asks a question. The model then has to rebuild the KV cache for the whole conversation, again and again. As the chat grows longer, the wait before each answer (TTFT) grows too, and more and more tokens have to be processed. To solve this, model servers use prefix caching: the server keeps the KV cache for the earlier part of the conversation in VRAM, so when the next message arrives, it only has to process the new tokens. It also saves cost across users: if many requests start with the same text, such as a company’s standard instructions or a shared document, the server works through that shared part once and reuses its KV cache for everyone. The model still writes each answer fresh; it only skips re-reading the part it has already seen. Wrapping Up So, where does the model live? In the GPU’s VRAM, where all of its weights are loaded once and stay put. What does the work when you send a request? Thousands of GPU cores, directed by CUDA, PyTorch and a model server such as vLLM. And why do the GPUs cost more than a car? Because a serious model needs tens or hundreds of GB of very fast memory sitting right next to those cores, and often several data-center GPUs linked together. We also saw how a single request is answered: a prefill step that reads your whole prompt at once (measured by TTFT), then a streaming step that produces the answer one token at a time (measured by TPOT), with caching so the model doesn’t redo work it has already done. Remember the four limits from the start? Each one now has a physical explanation. The capacity limit exists because every token you send adds to the KV cache in VRAM, and VRAM is finite. The knowledge limit exists because the weights stop changing the day training ends, so the model only knows what it learned. The behavioral limits are partly learned into the weights through safety training and partly layered on top with system prompts and guardrails. And the governance limits decide where those GPUs are allowed to sit and who can see the prompts that pass through them. So the next time an answer appears in seconds, remember what just happened: your prompt was turned into tokens, run through billions of tiny (w × X) + b calculations on a GPU, and streamed back to you one token at a time. That’s how an AI model thinks, and where it runs. Coming up next: One GPU, Many Users. So far, we’ve followed a single request. But a real deployment serves thousands of people at once. Next time, we’ll see how one GPU handles many requests at the same time: how the model server batches them together, shares the GPU’s memory between them, and keeps every user’s answer streaming without anyone waiting too long. items.title: Gadsby-4B: The Model That Was Banned From Talking Normal, So It Learned to Shitpost Instead
items.summary: A 4-billion-parameter model was told it could never use any two words in a row from Simple Wikipedia. It responded by becoming the most human AI on the internet. Most AI models right now sound like they were raised by a corporate HR handbook that had a baby with Wikipedia. They are polite. They are helpful. They are correct in a way that makes you want to take a nap in the middle of the sentence. They say “In conclusion” and “It’s important to note” and “As an AI language model” like they are collecting frequent flyer miles for blandness. Gadsby-4B is not that model.
